content.overview: Article 101 provides for vacation of seats in Parliament: no person may be a member of both Houses; if elected to both, must choose one; dual membership of Parliament and a State Legislature is restricted; resignation is to the Chairman/Speaker; absence for sixty days without permission can lead to declaration of vacancy; and other cases as provided.
content.glance: No dual membership of both Houses; choose one if elected to both. Resignation to Chair. 60-day absence may vacate seat.
content.study:
Article 101 addresses:
- Prohibition on being a member of both Houses of Parliament; election to both requires a choice.
- Restrictions relating to membership of Parliament and of a State Legislature.
- Resignation by writing to the Chairman (RS) or Speaker (LS).
- If a member is absent from all meetings for a period of sixty days without permission of the House, the House may declare the seat vacant (with rules on computing the period).

Examination: dual-membership rule; resignation form; 60-day absence rule.

sections.heading: Key rules
sections.body:
1. No simultaneous membership of both Houses; choice required if elected to both.
2. Resignation in writing to Chairman/Speaker.
3. Absence for 60 days without permission → House may declare seat vacant.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain vacation of seats under Article 101.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 101 prohibits a person from being a member of both Houses of Parliament and requires a choice if elected to both. A member may resign by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman or the Speaker. If a member is absent from all meetings of the House for a period of sixty days without permission, the House may declare the seat vacant.

examTips: No dual House membership; resignation to Chair; 60-day absence.

keyTakeaways: Art 101: dual membership ban; resignation; 60-day absence vacancy.
